sources.title: Arithmetic: compounding 1% per day for 365 days
sources.reliability_notes: Computed with Python on 2026-10-18. Pure arithmetic: an illustration of compounding, not a measurement of real people.

claims.text: In an online experiment with 14,341 participants, the same songs ended up with very different levels of success in separate groups when people could see what others downloaded.
caveats: Music downloads by volunteers; generalising to careers is an analogy.

claims.text: Quality still mattered in that experiment: the best songs rarely did badly and the worst rarely did well.
Improving by 1% a day for a year multiplies a starting value by about 37.8; declining by 1% a day leaves about 2.6% of it.
caveats: Arithmetic illustration, not data about real people; real growth is not a steady 1% a day.

claims.text: Sociologist Robert Merton named the Matthew effect: scientists who are already recognised tend to receive more credit for comparable work.
Economist Sherwin Rosen's model explains how, when one performer can serve a whole market, small differences in talent can produce very large differences in earnings.
caveats: A theoretical model, not an empirical measurement.

claims.text: A study of 633,263 researchers, entertainers, politicians and athletes found that individual performance follows a power-law distribution: a small group of top performers far outpaces the rest.
In a computer simulation of 40-year careers, the most successful agents were usually not the most talented but moderately talented and luckier.
caveats: A simulation, not observed careers; it doesn't show how much real success is luck.

claims.text: Taken together, this research suggests hard work pays most when it goes into skills and markets where gains build on themselves.
caveats: An interpretation of several studies, not a finding of any one of them.
